<reason>Both sides argued at a high level and the clash stayed tight and honest throughout. PRO (B) built a coherent case—panels select against unfamiliar work, the treadmill tax, accountability at the wrong timescale—and landed real blows: the Karikó "boomerang," the "lottery is an obituary for competition" exploitation of CON's own reform proposal, the Mill Hill answer to the pressure question, and the closing line that "a default cannot tell a dead lab from a daring one." But CON (A) controlled the decisive frame. The portability argument reclaimed Karikó convincingly (she survived on a colleague's independently won grant, then industry; under block funding that colleague's money flows through the same director), and the "asymmetry of default" weighing—competition ends dead labs by inaction while block funding requires a periodic hero—gave the judge a clean decision rule. CON also turned PRO's own "boom-bust" complaint against the claim that competition "never closes anything," and neutralized Mill Hill as a relocation rather than a closure. CON's closing concession—"every judge is fallible; the question is what happens after a judge is wrong"—resolved the Karikó dispute in a way PRO's "many doors, one gatekeeper" response did not fully answer, since PRO's pluralism requires a hiring committee before funding flows. A clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.3–A4.5): answering B's "competition has never closed anything" by pointing out non-renewal is money leaving by default—the very "boom-bust" PRO complained about—and reframing Mill Hill as money changing postcode, then crystallizing the "asymmetry of default" that made the accountability clash decidable.</best_rebuttal>
